ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: A total of 173 participants from the United States were initially enrolled and were recruited through social media platforms (e.g., Facebook, Instagram, Reddit).

Fifteen participants withdrew before or during the EMA phase, and three participants were excluded because they completed the EMA protocol outside the 21-day window due to scheduling conflicts, which would have introduced inconsistency in the temporal structure of the data, resulting in a final analytic sample of 155 (M age = 35.73, SD = 12.34).
At each prompt, participants were asked to recall the most emotionally salient situation they had experienced in the past three hours, which anchored all subsequent ratings.
Participants completed 12,011 of 13,020 scheduled prompts (92.3%; perparticipant range = 62-84 of 84; median = 80).
Participants were compensated US$40 for completing at least 80% of the surveys and US$60 for completing at least 95%.

Differences in measurement may also contribute: we assessed whether participants had used rumination in response to a salient situation during the preceding three hours, whereas prior work assessed the ruminative quality of ongoing thought at the moment of assessment.

> At each prompt, participants were asked to recall the most emotionally salient situation they had experienced in the past three hours, which anchored all subsequent ratings.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

Participants were compensated US$40 for completing at least 80% of the surveys and US$60 for completing at least 95%.

info.title: Time and Situation in Emotion Regulation

author.affiliation:
Department of Psychological & Brain Sciences
								Boston University

text.text: Daily context is widely recognized as shaping emotion regulation (ER) strategy use, yet empirical work has largely focused on situational context, with limited evidence on temporal context, despite the fact that cognitive and affective resources relevant to ER fluctuate systematically across the day.
The present study used ecological momentary assessment to examine how temporal rhythms and situational contexts shape ER strategy use and whether their contributions are independent.

Strategies were organized into approach-and avoidance-oriented orientations (e.g., reappraisal vs. distraction) to capture theoretically meaningful differences in regulatory goals and cognitive demands.
Over 21 days, 155 adults completed 4 daily prompts assessing situations and ER strategy use (12,011 observations).
Multilevel models indicated that participants endorsed fewer approach-and avoidance-oriented ER strategies as the day progressed and on weekends than on weekdays.

Multilevel latent profile analyses identified four situational profiles (Positivity-engagement, Low-engagement, Negativity-engagement, and Structured-engagement contexts) that were associated with ER strategy use.
Approach-oriented strategies were most frequent in Structured-engagement contexts, although their difference from Negativity-engagement contexts depended on savoring.

Avoidance-oriented strategies were used more in Negativity-engagement and Low-engagement contexts and less in Positivity-engagement contexts than in Structured-engagement contexts, a pattern that held across alternative strategy groupings in sensitivity analyses.

Accounting for situational context improved model fit and attenuated the temporal differences by 45% to 79%, indicating substantial overlap between temporal patterning and differences in the situations encountered across the day, while a smaller evening decline in approach-oriented strategies remained after accounting for situational context.
These findings provide initial evidence to ground context-sensitive models of ER flexibility and suggest temporal and situational windows for future research on ER-focused intervention.
Emotion regulation (ER) is broadly defined as the process by which people consciously or automatically use strategies to modulate emotional responses to environmental demands (Gross, 2015).
text.formatted: Emotion regulation (ER) is broadly defined as the process by which people consciously or automatically use strategies to modulate emotional responses to environmental demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Gross, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: ER unfolds dynamically in daily life and plays a central role in psychological well-being and psychopathology (Aldao et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2025).
text.formatted: ER unfolds dynamically in daily life and plays a central role in psychological well-being and psychopathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Aldao et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Chen et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Building on this foundation, recent theoretical frameworks have emphasized the importance of considering context and flexibility in ER (Aldao, 2013; Aldao et al., 2015; Bonanno et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Building on this foundation, recent theoretical frameworks have emphasized the importance of considering context and flexibility in ER <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Aldao, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Aldao et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bonanno et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Evaluating such flexibility, however, requires first understanding the naturally occurring patterns of strategy use in daily life.

Many studies examined only situations as context and focused on a limited set of situational characteristics (Chen et al., 2024 (Chen et al., , 2026;; Springstein & English, 2023; Willroth et al., 2025), without simultaneously considering how the time of day could shape ER.
text.formatted: Many studies examined only situations as context and focused on a limited set of situational characteristics <ref type="bibr">(Chen et al., 2024</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Chen et al., , 2026;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Springstein & English, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Willroth et al., 2025)</ref>, without simultaneously considering how the time of day could shape ER.

text.text: Addressing this gap can potentially improve our ability to explain why emotional crises tend to peak at night (Bu et al., 2025; Tubbs et al., 2022; Valtonen et al., 2006), to evaluate whether certain ER-context covariations constitute adaptive fit (Chen & Joormann, 2026), and to identify when and where ER-focused interventions are most needed (Bettis et al., 2022; Southward et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Addressing this gap can potentially improve our ability to explain why emotional crises tend to peak at night <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bu et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Tubbs et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Valtonen et al., 2006)</ref>, to evaluate whether certain ER-context covariations constitute adaptive fit <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Chen & Joormann, 2026)</ref>, and to identify when and where ER-focused interventions are most needed <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bettis et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Southward et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Understanding ER strategy use in daily contexts thus requires examining two fundamental contextual dimensions of daily life: the temporal context of the day and the situational context that arises alongside it.
One fundamental contextual dimension shaping ER strategy use in daily life is time.
Cognitive and affective resources relevant to ER fluctuate systematically across the day, shaped by circadian rhythms and daily routines.
Experience-sampling studies show reliable diurnal patterns in affective valence and arousal (Bu et al., 2025; Owens et al., 2000), and ER is typically engaged in response to affect (Gross, 2015).
text.formatted: Experience-sampling studies show reliable diurnal patterns in affective valence and arousal <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bu et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Owens et al., 2000)</ref>, and ER is typically engaged in response to affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Gross, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: It follows that the propensity to use different ER strategies may likewise vary as the day unfolds.

Consistent with this view, prior work has documented diurnal shifts in specific strategies, with reappraisal reported more frequently earlier in the day and rumination more commonly reported later (Moberly & Watkins, 2008; Takano & Tanno, 2011).
text.formatted: Consistent with this view, prior work has documented diurnal shifts in specific strategies, with reappraisal reported more frequently earlier in the day and rumination more commonly reported later <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Moberly & Watkins, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Takano & Tanno, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Despite these insights, it remains unclear whether the temporal dynamics of ER strategy use extend to broader motivational orientations, such as approach-versus avoidanceoriented strategies.
In addition to time, situational context plays a central role in shaping ER strategy use.
Situations can be understood as a fleeting set of external circumstances comprising cues that people perceive and interpret to form psychological meaning (Rauthmann & Sherman, 2020).
text.formatted: Situations can be understood as a fleeting set of external circumstances comprising cues that people perceive and interpret to form psychological meaning <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Rauthmann & Sherman, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These situational characteristics signal environmental demands and guide individuals in selecting strategies that best fit those demands (Guillaume et al., 2016; Rauthmann et al., 2014).
text.formatted: These situational characteristics signal environmental demands and guide individuals in selecting strategies that best fit those demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Guillaume et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Rauthmann et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: To systematically capture the psychological meaning of situations, Rauthmann and colleagues (2014) developed the DIAMONDS taxonomy, which identifies eight core situational characteristics: Duty, Intellect, Adversity, Mating, pOsitivity, Negativity, Deception, and Sociality.
text.formatted: To systematically capture the psychological meaning of situations, <ref type="bibr">Rauthmann and colleagues (2014)</ref> developed the DIAMONDS taxonomy, which identifies eight core situational characteristics: Duty, Intellect, Adversity, Mating, pOsitivity, Negativity, Deception, and Sociality.

text.text: More recent extensions have incorporated Controllability, given its central relevance to ER (Chen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: More recent extensions have incorporated Controllability, given its central relevance to ER <ref type="bibr">(Chen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This taxonomy provides a comprehensive framework for quantifying moment-to-moment situational context and examining how situational characteristics influence ER strategy use and emotions (Chen et al., 2024; Sherman et al., 2015).
text.formatted: This taxonomy provides a comprehensive framework for quantifying moment-to-moment situational context and examining how situational characteristics influence ER strategy use and emotions <ref type="bibr">(Chen et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Sherman et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: For example, social features of situations such as the presence of others and interpersonal demands are associated with differential strategy use, with suppression more likely when non-close others are present and when people pursue interpersonal goals (English et al., 2017).
text.formatted: For example, social features of situations such as the presence of others and interpersonal demands are associated with differential strategy use, with suppression more likely when non-close others are present and when people pursue interpersonal goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(English et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: However, prior work has examined individual DIAMONDS and Controllability dimensions in isolation.
Because situational characteristics tend to co-occur, examining them individually may not fully capture how situations are experienced as configurations of multiple psychological features.
Profilebased approaches provide a complementary way to represent such multivariate patterns by characterizing recurring combinations of features at the momentary level (Lee & Beck, 2026).
text.formatted: Profilebased approaches provide a complementary way to represent such multivariate patterns by characterizing recurring combinations of features at the momentary level <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Lee & Beck, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: A profile-based approach therefore allows us to examine whether ER differs across recurring configurations of situational characteristics, rather than estimating associations with each dimension separately.
Although temporal and situational contexts each shape ER strategy use, they may not be separable influences in daily life.
Daily experiences are often structured such that situations and their associated psychological characteristics tend to occur at particular times.

For example, Duty and Intellect demands are more common earlier in the day, whereas Sociality and pOsitivity situations more often emerge in evenings and on weekends (Bu et al., 2025; Marchand et al., 2016; Ryan et al., 2010).
text.formatted: For example, Duty and Intellect demands are more common earlier in the day, whereas Sociality and pOsitivity situations more often emerge in evenings and on weekends <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bu et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Marchand et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Ryan et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: This raises a key question: are temporal differences in ER strategy use fully explainable by momentary situational context?

They may jointly contribute to ER patterns: systematic shifts in situations across the day, and time-linked processes (e.g., circadian variation in cognitive control, fatigue) that operate independently of situational context.
Examining the degree of attenuation when situational context is added to temporal models may allow us to characterize the extent to which each source of context independently contributes to ER.

To examine how ER strategy use varies across temporal and situational contexts in a theoretically meaningful and statistically tractable way, we organize strategies into broad motivational orientations rather than examining them independently.
This categorization is particularly suited to ecological momentary assessment (EMA) designs.

First, individuals may report using none, one, or multiple strategies across assessments (Ford et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2026), which could lead to extremely high or low base rates at any given prompt, a problem that reduces statistical precision and inflates the number of simultaneous comparisons.

text.text: Aggregating strategies into orientations produces more stable count outcomes while preserving theoretically meaningful distinctions.

Second, motivational orientation captures a theoretically coherent dimension that is likely more sensitive to broad contextual pressures, such as the availability of cognitive resources or the nature of situational demands, than any individual strategy.

A longstanding distinction in ER and motivation literatures differentiates approach-oriented strategies (e.g., problem solving, reappraisal), which involve engaging with or modifying emotional experiences, from avoidance-oriented strategies (e.g., distraction, suppression), which involve disengaging from or attenuating emotional responses (Daniel et al., 2023; Kashdan et al., 2008).

text.text: This distinction is not intended to evaluate strategy effectiveness, but rather to capture differences in regulatory goals and cognitive demands that are likely sensitive to contextual constraints.

Organizing strategies by motivational orientation thus provides a theoretically grounded perspective for examining how temporal and situational contexts shape patterns of ER strategy use in daily life.
The present study used EMA over 21 days to examine how temporal and situational contexts shape the use of approach-and avoidance-oriented ER strategies in daily life.
Specifically, we aimed to address three main questions: a) How does the temporal context relate to approach-and avoidance-oriented ER strategy use?
b) How does situational context relate to these strategies?
c) Does accounting for situational context improve model fit and change observed temporal patterns in ER strategy use?
All three questions were exploratory.

For temporal context, individual ER strategies may follow different diurnal patterns because they rely on different cognitive, affective, and motivational processes (Moberly & Watkins, 2008; Takano & Tanno, 2011).
text.formatted: For temporal context, individual ER strategies may follow different diurnal patterns because they rely on different cognitive, affective, and motivational processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Moberly & Watkins, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Takano & Tanno, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Aggregating strategies into broader approach-and avoidance-oriented groups therefore does not imply a single directional pattern across the day.
For situational context, the profiles represent combinations of multiple situational characteristics, and different characteristics within a profile may point toward different regulatory responses.
We therefore examined how strategy orientations varied across these naturally occurring configurations rather than specifying directional predictions for particular profiles.
Finally, temporal and situational contexts may overlap while also contributing independently to ER strategy use.
We therefore examined how much the temporal associations changed after accounting for situational context, without specifying a particular magnitude of attenuation.
Together, these analyses characterize how ER strategy use is organized across the temporal and situational structure of daily life.

text.text: A total of 173 participants from the United States were initially enrolled and were recruited through social media platforms (e.g., Facebook, Instagram, Reddit).
Each participant attended an orientation meeting with a trained research assistant, during which the EMA procedure was explained and a practice survey was completed.

Fifteen participants withdrew before or during the EMA phase, and three participants were excluded because they completed the EMA protocol outside the 21-day window due to scheduling conflicts, which would have introduced inconsistency in the temporal structure of the data, resulting in a final analytic sample of 155 (M age = 35.73, SD = 12.34).
The sample was predominantly female (72.9%), with 3.9% identifying as non-binary or gender non-conforming.

Most participants identified as Caucasian American (49.0%), followed by Asian American (27.7%), Black or African American (12.9%), American Indian, Alaska Native, or Native Hawaiian (2.6%), and multiracial (5.2%), and 10.3% identified as Hispanic or Latino.

text.text: During the 21-day EMA period, participants received four daily prompts at approximately 12 PM, 3 PM, 6 PM, and 9 PM, with up to 90 minutes to respond.
At each prompt, participants were asked to recall the most emotionally salient situation they had experienced in the past three hours, which anchored all subsequent ratings.
Across the four prompts, the recall windows therefore spanned approximately 9 AM to 9 PM.

This schedule was established by the parent study to provide evenly spaced coverage across daytime and evening hours while limiting participant burden over the 21-day EMA period and avoiding later-night assessments.

Because the parent study was designed to assess ER flexibility across everyday situations rather than circadian variation across the full day, early-morning and late-night periods were not sampled (see Limitations).
Participants completed 12,011 of 13,020 scheduled prompts (92.3%; perparticipant range = 62-84 of 84; median = 80).
Participants were compensated US$40 for completing at least 80% of the surveys and US$60 for completing at least 95%.

Momentary ER Strategy Use.
Following the situational ratings, participants indicated whether they used a series of ER strategies as 0 (no) or 1 (yes) based on their response to the situation.
Participants could endorse multiple strategies per prompt.

Strategies included cognitive reappraisal (i.e., I changed how I thought about the event), expressive suppression (i.e., I made sure to hide how I feel), rumination (i.e., I repeatedly thought about the event and could not stop), worry (i.e., I worried about what may happen), distraction (i.e., I did something else to take my mind off it), problem-solving (i.e., I tried to solve problems or resolve the events), savoring (i.e., I took time to savor or enjoy what happened), planning (i.e., I made plans for the next steps), positive refocusing (i.e., I focused on the positive aspect of the event), soothing (i.e., I looked to others for comfort), and perspective seeking (i.e., I tried to find out what others would do if they were in my situation).

Following previous studies (Bischof et al., 2024; Daniel et al., 2019; Daros et al., 2019; Hohensee et al., 2025), strategies were classified into two motivational orientations: approach-oriented ER strategies (i.e., cognitive reappraisal, savoring, problem-solving, planning, and perspective seeking) and avoidance-oriented ER strategies (i.e., distraction, rumination, expressive suppression, soothing, worry, and positive refocusing).

No strategy or situational item was missing at any completed prompt.

Bayesian R² increased modestly when situational context was added (approach-oriented ER strategy use: 0.47 to 0.51; avoidance-oriented ER strategy use: 0.47 to 0.52), indicating that situational context accounted for additional variance in ER strategy use beyond temporal predictors alone.

The relatively large ΔELPD values alongside modest R² increments reflect the fact that the Bayesian R² captures total variance explained-including the substantial betweenperson component, whereas ELPD differences are sensitive to within-person predictive improvements; these metrics are thus complementary rather than contradictory.

text.text: Consistent with the lack of a uniform structure in prior work, the multilevel exploratory factor analysis of the 11 binary strategy items (Supplemental Results) did not recover an approach-avoidance structure at either level.

Within persons, a two-factor solution fit adequately (comparative fit index [CFI] = .94, root mean square error of approximation [RMSEA] = .053) and distinguished a positive-focus factor, defined primarily by savoring (.92) and positive refocusing (.98), from a broader factor on which most of the remaining strategies loaded.

A three-factor solution fit better (CFI = .98, RMSEA = .040), further separating a problem-oriented factor (problem solving = .80, planning = .83, reappraisal = .35) from a third factor characterized by soothing (.74), perspective seeking (.70), rumination (.56), and worry (.42).
Between persons, a general factor on which most strategies loaded, together with the same positive-focus factor (savoring = .89, positive refocusing = .97), described the data well (CFI = .997).

The central finding of this study is that temporal patterns in regulatory behavior largely reflect the situations people encounter at different times of day: temporal and situational contexts overlap substantially, and much of the temporal patterning was accounted for by the changing composition of situations across the day and week.
Three findings emerged.

First, both approachand avoidance-oriented ER strategies declined from daytime to evening and were less frequently used on weekends than on weekdays, indicating that the number of strategies endorsed is temporally patterned.
Second, ER strategy use differed across situational profiles.

Relative to Structured-engagement contexts, approach-oriented strategies were less frequent in Lowengagement and Positivity-engagement contexts, whereas the difference in Negativityengagement contexts depended on savoring.

Avoidance-oriented strategies were more frequent in Negativity-engagement and Low-engagement contexts and less frequent in Positivityengagement contexts, a pattern that remained across alternative strategy groupings.

Third, after accounting for situational context, the 9 PM versus 12 PM differences were attenuated by approximately 45% to 66% and the weekend differences by approximately 53% to 79%, indicating substantial overlap between temporal patterning and the changing composition of situations across the day and week.
A smaller evening decline in approach-oriented strategy use nevertheless remained after accounting for situational context.

Both approach-and avoidance-oriented strategy use declined from daytime to evening and was lower on weekends than on weekdays, consistent with prior evidence that affective and cognitive processes vary across the day (e.g., Bu et al., 2025; Owens et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Both approach-and avoidance-oriented strategy use declined from daytime to evening and was lower on weekends than on weekdays, consistent with prior evidence that affective and cognitive processes vary across the day (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Bu et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Owens et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: The decline concerned how many listed strategies were endorsed rather than whether any listed strategy of either orientation was endorsed: the probability of endorsing at least one strategy of either orientation did not differ by time of day or day of week, and the two orientations declined in parallel rather than one replacing the other.
The decline also did not apply to every strategy: savoring and positive refocusing increased rather than decreased across the day and on weekends.

Additionally, rumination declined across the sampled period, in contrast to prior studies that have reported nonlinear diurnal patterns in ruminative self-focus, including increases later in the day (Moberly & Watkins, 2008; Takano & Tanno, 2011).
text.formatted: Additionally, rumination declined across the sampled period, in contrast to prior studies that have reported nonlinear diurnal patterns in ruminative self-focus, including increases later in the day <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Moberly & Watkins, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Takano & Tanno, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Differences in temporal coverage may partly explain this discrepancy.
The present assessments extended to 9 PM, whereas prior work sampled across a broader portion of participants' waking day and captured later-evening periods in which rumination may increase.

Differences in measurement may also contribute: we assessed whether participants had used rumination in response to a salient situation during the preceding three hours, whereas prior work assessed the ruminative quality of ongoing thought at the moment of assessment.

Temporal patterns in rumination may therefore depend on both the portion of the waking day sampled and the form of rumination being assessed, and sampling across a broader portion of the waking day would be needed to determine whether rumination increases later in the evening.
Two factors may contribute to this overall decline.

First, cognitive and task-related demands may be more concentrated earlier in the day (Marchand et al., 2016; Owens et al., 2000; Ryan et al., 2010), such that later situations prompt fewer strategies.

text.text: Weekend reductions in ER strategy use further support this idea: weekdays may impose greater task demands and interpersonal obligations that call for regulation, whereas weekends may involve less structured demands and situations that prompt fewer strategies (Marchand et al., 2016; Ryan et al., 2010).

text.text: The attenuation analysis is consistent with this explanation for a substantial part of the diurnal decline and of the weekend difference.

Second, evening reductions may reflect regulatory fatigue (or mental fatigue), depletion of motivational and cognitive resources following sustained demands across the day (Herlambang et al., 2021; Lewczuk et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Second, evening reductions may reflect regulatory fatigue (or mental fatigue), depletion of motivational and cognitive resources following sustained demands across the day <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Herlambang et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Lewczuk et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, fatigue, sleep, chronotype, and cognitive control were not directly assessed, and the sampling window did not extend into late-night hours.
These possibilities therefore cannot be distinguished from other time-linked processes in the present data.
Future research incorporating momentary measures of fatigue would help clarify the relative contributions of these processes.
Differences in how specific forms of regulation relate to context emerge more clearly at the situational level, as discussed below.
MLPA identified four psychologically meaningful situational profiles that were differentially associated with ER strategy use.

In the primary classification, approach-oriented strategies were most frequent in Structured-engagement contexts, which were characterized by high Duty, pOsitivity, and Controllability and low Negativity, and were less frequent in Positivity-engagement, Low-engagement, and Negativity-engagement contexts.
However, the sensitivity analyses showed that the association with Negativity-engagement contexts depended on savoring.

Once savoring was removed, the remaining approach-oriented strategies (problem solving, planning, reappraisal, and perspective seeking), taken together, were more frequent in Negativity-engagement than in Structured-engagement contexts, whereas the reductions in Lowengagement and Positivity-engagement contexts remained.
Among the individual strategies, this was driven mainly by problem solving.
These findings suggest that the primary approachoriented composite brought together strategies that share an engagement orientation but respond differently to the content of the situation.

Problem solving, planning, reappraisal, and perspective seeking involve acting on, modifying, or working through a situation and may therefore be used when situations make salient demands, including negative ones (Ford & Troy, 2019; Troy et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Problem solving, planning, reappraisal, and perspective seeking involve acting on, modifying, or working through a situation and may therefore be used when situations make salient demands, including negative ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Ford & Troy, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Troy et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, their greater use in Negativity-engagement contexts suggests that negative situational intensity did not reduce the use of these strategies in the present data, contrasting with experimental evidence that high emotional intensity can shift preferences away from reappraisal toward disengagement (Sheppes et al., 2011).

text.text: Savoring, by contrast, involves engaging with positive experience and was concentrated in more positive situational contexts (Bryant & Veroff, 2017; Fredrickson, 2004).

text.text: Thus, the motivational distinction between engaging with and disengaging from a situation captures only part of how strategies differed across contexts; the valence of what is being engaged with also appears important.
Avoidance-oriented strategies showed a more consistent situational pattern.
They were more frequent in Negativity-engagement and Low-engagement contexts and less frequent in Positivity-engagement contexts relative to Structured-engagement contexts.

The higher number of avoidance-oriented strategies endorsed in Negativity-engagement contexts is broadly consistent with evidence that disengagement-oriented responses become more likely as negative emotional intensity increases (Sheppes et al., 2011).
text.formatted: The higher number of avoidance-oriented strategies endorsed in Negativity-engagement contexts is broadly consistent with evidence that disengagement-oriented responses become more likely as negative emotional intensity increases <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Sheppes et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: This pattern did not depend on the placement of any single contested strategy.

It became stronger when positive refocusing and soothing were removed from the avoidance-oriented grouping and was also evident when distraction and suppression and rumination and worry were examined separately.

The situational association for avoidance-oriented strategy use therefore appears comparatively robust across alternative ways of organizing the strategies, although these findings concern the number of strategies endorsed rather than the likelihood of using any strategy of that orientation.
A broader pattern emerged across the sensitivity analyses and the multilevel exploratory factor analysis.

Savoring and positive refocusing were concentrated in Positivity-engagement and Structured-engagement contexts, were relatively uncommon in Negativity-engagement and Low-engagement contexts, and formed a distinct positive-focus factor at both levels of the factor analysis.
They also differed from most other strategies temporally, increasing rather than decreasing across the day.
By comparison, the groupings that exclude savoring and positive refocusing, approach-and avoidance-oriented alike, were more frequent in Negativityengagement than in Positivity-engagement contexts.

This suggests that strategy organization in daily life reflects not only whether regulation involves engagement or disengagement but also whether the strategy is directed toward positive or negative emotional content.

This interpretation is consistent with evidence that strategies also cluster by the content they engage with, as in the separation of aversive cognitive perseveration from adaptive engagement (Naragon-Gainey et al., 2017), and with factor analyses in which savoring and social support separate from other strategies at the within-person level (McMahon & Naragon-Gainey, 2019; Southward & Cheavens, 2020).

text.text: The approach-and avoidance-oriented composites therefore remain useful for organizing broad motivational tendencies, but their associations should be interpreted alongside the component strategies and the alternative groupings examined here, and none of these patterns implies that a particular strategy-context combination is more adaptive.

Between-person differences in stable situational exposure showed minimal associations with ER strategy use, consistent with prior work showing that most variance in strategy use occurs within rather than across individuals (Brans et al., 2013; English et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Between-person differences in stable situational exposure showed minimal associations with ER strategy use, consistent with prior work showing that most variance in strategy use occurs within rather than across individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brans et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">English et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The present findings therefore point more strongly to moment-to-moment situational variation than to stable differences in the types of situations people typically encounter.
In this sense, momentary context is associated both with how many strategies are endorsed and with which strategies are used.
Incorporating situational context substantially improved model fit.

Holding situational composition constant reduced the evening decline by about half for approach-oriented strategies and by about two-thirds for avoidance-oriented strategies, and reduced the weekend differences by roughly half to four-fifths.
Temporal and situational contexts therefore overlap substantially rather than contributing fully independently.
The descriptive data illustrate this overlap:

Negativity-engagement and Structured-engagement contexts became less common and Positivity-engagement contexts more common over the day and on weekends, and these shifts matter because the situational profiles differed systematically in the number and types of strategies endorsed.

What remains after adjustment is a smaller evening decline in approachoriented strategies (rate ratio 0.93 at 9 PM) and no reliable residual difference for avoidanceoriented strategies or for weekends.

The residual decline suggests that time-linked processes such as fatigue may contribute to approach-oriented regulation even after situational composition is taken into account, but the present design cannot identify them.

Together, these results speak to all three motivating questions raised before: the evening decline in approach-oriented strategies that remained after adjusting for situational composition is consistent with reports that emotional crises peak in the evening (Bu et al., 2025; Tubbs et al., 2022; Valtonen et al., 2006), although our sampling ended at 9 PM; the situational asymmetry between approach-and avoidance-oriented strategy use offers descriptive benchmarks that future work could use to evaluate what constitutes adaptive ER-context fit (Chen & Joormann, 2026); and the finding that avoidance-oriented strategies were most frequent in Negativity-engagement contexts and that approach-oriented strategies were fewest in Low-engagement contexts identifies the contexts where studies measuring regulatory need and outcomes should look first when evaluating when and where ER-focused support might matter (Southward et al., 2021).

text.text: While our study provides important contributions, it also has limitations.
Most fundamentally, the explanatory adjustment framework adopted here does not support causal inference (Maxwell & Cole, 2007).
text.formatted: Most fundamentally, the explanatory adjustment framework adopted here does not support causal inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Maxwell & Cole, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Situational characteristics and ER strategy use were assessed contemporaneously within the same EMA prompt, meaning we cannot establish that situational exposure temporally preceded strategy selection.

Future research should employ designs that permit temporal ordering, such as lagged multilevel models or experimental situational manipulations, to better clarify the directionality of these associations.
Second, we used four fixed EMA prompts per day, with recall windows spanning approximately 9 AM to 9 PM.
This design may have missed rapid shifts in situational experience and emotional responses and did not capture early-morning or late-night periods.
In addition, prompts were anchored to clock time, while wake time, chronotype, and work schedules were not assessed.

As a result, the same prompt could occur at different points in the waking day for individuals with earlier versus later schedules, and the present design cannot distinguish clock-time patterns from variation associated with individual circadian timing.
The present findings should therefore be interpreted as patterns across the sampled clock-time window rather than as a complete circadian course of ER strategy use.

Future studies could use burst sampling, random-time prompting, or assessment schedules that extend across a broader portion of the waking day and incorporate wake time, chronotype, and work schedules so that temporal effects can also be examined relative to each person's daily rhythm (Ladis et al., 2023; Marciniak et al., 2024; Schricker et al., 2023).

text.text: Third, the sample was not demographically representative, with a predominance of White and female participants.
Future studies should replicate these findings in more diverse populations and across cultural contexts (Chen et al., 2025; Chen & Soto, 2024).
text.formatted: Future studies should replicate these findings in more diverse populations and across cultural contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Chen et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Chen & Soto, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Lastly, situational characteristics and ER strategies were assessed with single-item measures, which may limit psychometric precision.

Individuals often engage in multiple ER strategies within a single situation or across time (Ford et al., 2019; Hartmann et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026) and they may also experience mixed emotions in response to a given situation (Larsen et al., 2001; Larsen & McGraw, 2014; S. M. Li et al., 2026).

text.text: Future research should model within-person variability in ER strategy use and transitions between strategies over time and examine ER in the context of mixed emotional experiences.
Despite these limitations, the present findings offer important implications for both theory and future clinical research.

Much of the ER flexibility literature has emphasized adaptive strategy selection in response to situational context, yet descriptive evidence regarding when and under what conditions strategies are actually used in daily life remains limited (Bonanno et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024).

text.text: Because much of the temporal variation reflected shifts in situational exposure, with only a small residual evening decline, future models of ER flexibility may need to consider how the temporal structure of the day organizes the situations people encounter.
The sensitivity and factor analyses further suggest that such models should consider the emotional content a strategy engages with, not only its motivational orientation.
These findings may also have clinical implications for the timing of ER assessment and intervention.
The residual evening decline in approach-oriented strategy endorsement suggests that time of day may be relevant to how people regulate their emotions, even after accounting for situational context.

However, the present study did not assess fatigue, regulatory goals or resources, strategy effectiveness, subsequent affect, distress, or impairment, so it cannot determine whether this temporal pattern reflects greater regulatory difficulty or clinical vulnerability later in the day.
Future research should test whether these patterns are more pronounced in clinical populations and whether they correspond to periods of greater regulatory difficulty.
Establishing these links would be necessary before using temporal patterns in ER strategy use to inform when ER-focused interventions are delivered.

This study provides initial evidence that the number of ER strategies people endorse in daily life varies with both temporal and situational context, and that these two sources of context overlap substantially.
Participants endorsed fewer approach-and avoidance-oriented strategies later in the day and on weekends, whereas whether any strategy of either orientation was endorsed did not differ.
Much of this decline reflected the situations people were in at those times.
With situational composition held constant, the evening and weekend differences were smaller by about half or more, and only a small evening decline in approach-oriented strategies remained.

Across situations, approach-oriented strategies were most common in Structuredengagement contexts and least common in Low-engagement contexts, whereas avoidanceoriented strategies were most common in Negativity-engagement contexts and least common in Positivity-engagement contexts.
The avoidance-oriented pattern held across alternative strategy groupings, whereas the approach-oriented pattern depended on how savoring was grouped.

Together, these findings indicate that temporal patterns in ER strategy use cannot be interpreted without reference to the situations that occupy different times of day, and they provide descriptive benchmarks for future work on when and where people regulate.
